content: Emergency contraception (EC), also known as emergency postcoital contraception, refers to methods used to prevent pregnancy after sexual intercourse. These methods are designed for occasional use, particularly in situations where primary contraceptive methods fail. Since EC methods act before implantation of a fertilized egg, they are classified medically and legally as contraceptives. However, some pro-life groups, which define pregnancy as beginning at fertilization, consider EC to be abortifacient. Interest in synthetic hormones as postcoital contraceptives began several decades ago, with the first published study on the topic appearing in 1967. Early research focused on high-dose estrogens, with the initial hope that postcoital contraception could serve as a viable ongoing contraceptive method. Emergency contraceptive pills (ECPs), often referred to as morning-after pills, are medications that work by preventing ovulation or fertilization and may also inhibit the implantation of a fertilized egg (blastocyst). These pills typically contain higher doses of the same hormones (estrogens, progestins, or both) found in regular combined oral contraceptives. Another type of ECP, mifepristone, is an anti-hormonal drug that does not contain estrogen or progestins. Despite the term morning-after pill, ECPs are approved for use up to 72 hours after unprotected intercourse. It is important to note that ECPs are distinct from medical abortion methods, which act after implantation. Intrauterine devices (IUDs), while primarily used as a regular contraceptive method, can also serve as emergency contraception. The copper-T IUD, for example, can be inserted up to five days after unprotected intercourse to prevent pregnancy. IUDs are more effective than ECPs when used as emergency contraception, with pregnancy rates comparable to those seen with regular IUD use. Additionally, IUDs can remain in place after the subsequent menstrual cycle to provide ongoing contraception for 3 to 10 years, depending on the type of device.
